name: Leg curl
angleNote: Knee flexion: 0° = leg straight (start), 120° = heel towards the buttocks. Hip at the origin.

segments.massNote: Segment mass as a fraction of body mass, and centre of mass as a fraction of the segment length from its proximal end. Approximate textbook anthropometry. The lower leg includes the foot.
segments.massSource: TODO: check against a published anthropometric table (e.g. Dempster's segment parameters as tabulated by Winter)
segments.note: Hip→knee and knee→ankle in metres, typical adult.

strengthCurve.label: Knee flexor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative knee-flexion torque vs knee angle, assumed strongest with the knee straight. One curve for every variant, although the hamstrings are longer (stronger) seated with the hip bent. Approximate shape.
strengthCurve.source: TODO: verify against published torque–angle data

muscles.name: Hamstrings
muscles.note: Cross the hip as well; their length (and strength) depends on hip angle, which these weights ignore.

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius
muscles.note: Calf muscle that also crosses the knee and helps flex it.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Lying or standing with an ankle weight, the lower leg passes horizontal near 90°, where gravity's torque peaks.

phases.name: Fully bent
phases.text: Heel near the buttocks; hamstrings are weakest here.

variants.name: Lying leg curl machine

camProfile.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight, including any lever or pulley ratio. Illustrative shape, not measured from a specific machine.
camProfile.source: TODO: replace with a measured profile for a real machine

variants.notes: Face down with the hip straight. The pad is behind the ankle; lifting the lower leg's weight also adds torque until it passes vertical (90°).

variants.name: Seated leg curl machine

camProfile.note: Effective radius in metres: joint torque per unit of stack weight, including any lever or pulley ratio. Illustrative shape, not measured from a specific machine.
camProfile.source: TODO: replace with a measured profile for a real machine

variants.notes: Hip bent 90°, so the hamstrings work from a longer length. Here the lower leg's weight helps the curl. The extra strength from the longer hamstrings is not modelled.

variants.name: Standing leg curl (ankle weight)
variants.notes: Torque = (m·L + lower-leg weight)·g·sin(knee angle): nothing at the start, largest with the lower leg horizontal at 90°.
